summary.text: After Eurydice was lost a second time, Orpheus sat in an enchanted grove where trees and beasts gathered to hear him — and from his lyre sang the loves of the gods: Ganymede borne away by Jove in eagle form, and Hyacinth slain by Apollo's discus, from whose blood the flower sprang marked with AI, AI.

chapters.title: The enchanted grove
chapters.text: Orpheus drew together a grove where no sun beat too harshly — oak and linden, beech and laurel, and all the trees that once had been men and women. Tigers lay with sheep, and the lynx with the hare; birds and serpents came to listen. There he sat among the animals and tuned his lyre, vowing gentler songs than when he sang of giants on Phlegra: now he would sing of boys beloved of gods, and maids who paid the penalty of wrong.

chapters.title: Ganymede
chapters.text: First he sang how Jove, burning for the Phrygian boy Ganymede, took no shape but the eagle's — strong enough to bear his thunderbolts — and stole the Trojan from Ida to pour nectar in the cups of the gods on Olympus, to Juno's lasting anger.

chapters.title: Hyacinth
chapters.text: Then Apollo and Hyacinth, stripped and oiled for sport, cast the discus — and the boy, rushing for glory, was struck as the disc rebounded from the earth. The god could not heal him; from his blood arose a flower like a lily but purple, and on its petals Apollo inscribed the letters of his grief: AI, AI. Sparta still honours Hyacinthus with solemn festival.
